paper.title: HieraSparse: Hierarchical Semi-Structured Sparse KV Attention
paper.abstract: The deployment of long-context LLMs poses significant challenges due to the intense computational cost of self-attention and substantial memory overhead of the KV cache. We introduce HieraSparse, a hierarchical KV cache compression framework with acceleration kernels that leverage GPU Sparse Tensor Cores to speed up semi-structured KV cache attention for both prefill and decode phases. With hierarchical design, our method allows for flexible quality-sparsity trade-off and successfully converts sparsity into efficiency. Compared to state-of-the-art decode method that utilizes unstructured sparsity, HieraSparse achieves 1.2× KV compression ratio and 4.57× attention speedup at the same sparsity level. Furthermore, we extended semi-structured KV cache pruning to the prefill stage, which demonstrated up to 1.85× attention speedup at the highest sparsity. Lastly, we evaluate generation quality of HieraSparse with a simple magnitude-based pruning method, and the results show that 1.37× prefill speedup and 1.77× decode speedup can be achieved without significant quality drop.

paper.title: FastInfer: Breaking the Low-to-Moderate Sparsity Barrier for Efficient LLM Inference
paper.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) continue to scale, unstructured pruning has become a key technique for reducing inference cost. However, to preserve model quality, pruning is typically limited to low-to-moderate sparsity (30%–60%), where existing GPU-based sparse inference frameworks often fail to deliver consistent speedups over dense baselines. This paper proposes FastInfer, a new sparse LLM inference framework in the low-to-moderate sparsity regime. FastInfer introduces a novel thread-centric encoding paradigm that rethinks sparse computation on Tensor Core Units from the perspective of per-thread register requirements. Based on this, we design the TFBE format, which enables low-overhead operand reconstruction. FastInfer integrates an affinity-aware data-movement mechanism and a triple-stage pipeline to better exploit modern GPU features and improve pipeline utilization. Compared with the state-of-the-art SpInfer, FastInfer achieves geometric-mean speedups of 1.52x (up to 2.1x) for sparse kernels and 1.27x (up to 1.42x) for end-to-end sparse inference on H100.

paper.title: Pushing the Envelope of LLM Inference with Ultra-Low-Bit Quantized Models
paper.abstract: The advent of ultra-low-bit LLM models, approaching the perplexity and task accuracy of their full-precision counterparts, is ushering in a new era of LLM inference. While these advances promise models that are cost-effective in latency, memory, throughput, and energy consumption, the runtime efficiency for deploying ultra-low-bit models remains under-explored. We take a bottom-up approach: we first implement 2-bit microkernels for modern CPUs, achieving close-to-roofline performance. We integrate these microkernels into LLM inference pipelines and present end-to-end results with 2-bit models, outperforming the state-of-the-art (SOTA) bitnet.cpp runtime by 2.2x, and deliver up to 7x speedup over 16-bit inference. We extend this work to Intel Xe2 GPUs where we implement mixed-precision 2-bit kernels, and show their performance to be close-to-optimal. Integrated into the vLLM framework, these kernels deliver up to 6.7x speedup over the 16-bit end-to-end pipeline across a range of models and Xe2 GPUs, thus pushing the envelope of LLM inference.

paper.title: BaGuaLu-2: Taming Dynamic Memory Fluctuation for Efficient MoE Model Training Over 10,000 GPUs
paper.abstract: Fine-grained Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is the de facto architecture for scaling large language models. However, dynamic expert load imbalance causes severe memory fluctuations, degrading training efficiency. Existing systems rely on static memory provisioning: they either over-provision, leaving GPU memory idle during normal execution, or under-provision, inviting out-of-memory crashes and costly manual rollbacks when load spikes occur. To address these challenges, we propose BaGuaLu-2, a large-scale MoE training system that eliminates this dilemma through flexible provisioning. By transforming memory allocation from a static, one-time tuning choice into a continuous and fine-grained control, BaGuaLu-2 grants exact activation memory on demand for each training batch. Furthermore, it offsets any dynamic management overhead through system optimizations. BaGuaLu-2 demonstrates exceptional scalability, training a model with 1,040 billion parameters across 12,288 GPUs while sustaining over 2 EFlops at 35% MFU. Compared with state-of-the-art systems, BaGuaLu-2 delivers 1.14× and 1.13× average throughput improvements over Megatron-Kwai and AdaPipe, respectively.

paper.title: Every Microsecond Matters: Achieving Near-Speed-of-Light Latency in GPU Collectives
paper.abstract: GPU collective communication is often optimized for bandwidth, yet many emerging workloads are latency-bound. Long-context LLM inference is a key example, where small collectives lie on the critical path of token generation, making microsecond-scale overheads impactful. In this work, we study how to approach the hardware speed-of-light (SoL) lower bound for GPU collectives within a scale-up network. We identify key design principles, including barrier-free synchronization and efficient use of symmetric memory and multicast. Building on NCCL’s device-side API, we develop low-latency interfaces for constructing custom kernels and implement new symmetric collectives in NCCL. Microbenchmarks show substantial latency reductions, achieving within 10% of the measured SoL bound. Integrated into applications, these kernels reduce inter-token latency and improve throughput in LLM inference, while also accelerating cuSOLVERMp, demonstrating benefits across AI and HPC workloads.

paper.title: CoreFlow: Context-Centric Resource Management for LLM-Based Agentic Workflows
paper.abstract: The rise of agentic workflows, which coordinate multiple LLM-based agents to tackle complex tasks, has shifted the LLM serving toward a multi-step, context-driven execution paradigm. This shift introduces highly skewed context-length distributions and agent-specific KV cache-reuse patterns in LLM workloads, challenging existing resource management systems that remain oblivious to these characteristics. This paper introduces CoreFlow, a context-centric resource management system tailored for the distinct execution patterns of agentic workflows. CoreFlow incorporates three key designs: (1) hierarchical performance modeling, which captures the effects of context-length variance and imbalanced cache reuse inherent in context-driven execution; (2) dual-level resource optimization, combining workflow-level allocation to distribute resources across agents with agent-level partitioning to isolate requests with heterogeneous context lengths; and (3) adaptive cache management, which aligns cache placement with resource partitioning while minimizing cache-swap overhead. Evaluations on representative workflows demonstrate that CoreFlow reduces end-to-end latency by 57.6% and improves workflow throughput by 63.1%.

paper.title: Prefill-Decode Aggregation or Disaggregation? Unifying Both for Goodput-Optimized LLM Serving
paper.abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving has long centered on a debate between prefill-decode (PD) aggregation and disaggregation. We systematically compare them under joint time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-per-output-token (TPOT) service-level objectives (SLOs): aggregation wins when TTFT SLOs are tight and TPOT SLOs relaxed; disaggregation wins in the opposite regime. Under balanced SLOs, however, both are significantly suboptimal in SLO-compliant throughput (goodput), revealing a previously uncharacterized gap. We attribute this gap to unexploited latency slack: many requests complete well within SLOs while others approach violation. We propose latency shifting, a design principle for reallocating SLO slack across requests and phases to maximize goodput. TaiChi, an LLM serving system, unifies aggregation and disaggregation through hybrid-mode inference to realize this principle through flowing decode and length-aware prefill scheduling. TaiChi improves goodput by up to 40% and reduces P90 TTFT and TPOT by up to 5.3× and 1.6×, respectively, over state-of-the-art aggregation and disaggregation systems.

paper.title: When KV Meets Embeddings: Dynamic GPU Memory Allocation for Accelerating Generative Recommender Serving
paper.abstract: Generative recommender (GR) inference faces a dual memory bottleneck absent in LLM serving. Embedding hot caches and KV caches compete for limited GPU HBM, while existing systems optimize them in isolation, leading to suboptimal tail latency. We observe that (1) the optimal EMB–KV memory allocation ratio shifts by up to 0.35 across workloads, and (2) static allocations leave 20%–30% latency improvement untapped, while continuous reallocation risks cache thrashing and P99 SLO violations. We present RACER, which jointly and adaptively allocates HBM at runtime. It addresses two challenges: (1) adaptive memory allocation via a three-layer PPO controller with online adaptation and burst recovery, achieving 32 μs decision latency; and (2) embedding-KV-aware scheduling that maximizes joint EMB–KV cache reuse across nodes. Evaluations on three production-scale datasets show that RACER reduces P99 latency by 24%–38% over the best static strategy and achieves 93.5%–99.6% SLO satisfaction, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines (67%–94.2%) without sacrificing throughput.

paper.title: Efficient Serving for Agentic LLM Workflows via Micro-Task-Level Parallelism
paper.abstract: Agentic large language model (LLM) workflows leverage the advanced capabilities of LLMs to instantiate a multi-agent paradigm, where each LLM invocation constitutes an agentic task. Existing optimizations rely on coarse-grained task-level scheduling, which fails to exploit fine-grained parallelism within the workflow, leading to resource underutilization and bursty latency. In this paper, we present Grape, a full-stack LLM system for serving agentic LLM workflows that fully exploits micro-task (μTask)-level parallelism. On the frontend, Grape proposes the TaskFlow abstraction to provide a declarative interface for workflow orchestration. Subsequently, Grape decomposes tasks represented in TaskFlow into fine-grained μTasks that expose the parallelism within the workflow. For the LLM engine, Grape adopts a μTasks-aware scheduling policy with SLO-derived constraints to ensure low-latency execution with improved resource utilization. Moreover, Grape also proposes a dedicated memory management mechanism to alleviate KV Cache memory pressure. The experimental results demonstrate the superiority of Grape over state-of-the-art solutions.

paper.title: MIST: A Co-Design Framework for Heterogeneous, Multi-Stage LLM Inference
paper.abstract: Modern LLM serving spans multi-stage pipelines, including RAG retrieval and KV cache reuse, with distinct compute, memory, and latency demands. Inference engines expose vast configuration spaces with no systematic navigation methodology, and exhaustive benchmarking can exceed $40K in cloud costs. Meanwhile, hardware is diversifying across AMD GPUs, TPUs, and custom ASICs, yet cross-vendor prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation lacks a unified software stack for end-to-end evaluation. We present MIST, an event-driven simulation framework that models the full serving stack across AI workload, system and software, and hardware layers, with pluggable accelerator models enabling cross-vendor evaluation. MIST achieves end-to-end fidelity within 6% of real deployed systems. In design-space exploration case studies, under stated pricing and hardware assumptions, multi-vendor PD-disaggregated deployments identified by MIST yield up to 49.3% higher tokens/$ than single-vendor PD disaggregation. MIST also enables KV storage co-design, revealing how memory hierarchy choices shape tail latency. MIST is available at https://github.com/MIST-Simulator/MIST.

paper.title: BidKV: Utility-Guided Preemption Scheduling for KV-Pressure LLM Serving
paper.abstract: When key-value (KV) cache demand exceeds GPU memory in online large language model (LLM) serving, engines reclaim active requests' cache. Poor victim selection increases recomputation and time to first token (TTFT). We present BidKV, a utility-guided policy that ranks victims by recoverable capacity and estimated disruption cost. BidKV integrates with vLLM and SGLang through a portable adapter that reuses native preemption. With Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and ShareGPT traces, BidKV reduces 95th-percentile TTFT by over 90% and improves 300 ms service-level objective (SLO) attainment by 14.8 percentage points over vLLM's native policy. On SGLang, it reduces 95th-percentile TTFT by 94.6% and improves SLO attainment by 38.8 percentage points over native least-recently-used eviction. Source code is available at https://github.com/CGCL-codes/BidKV.

paper.title: Mercury: Practical User-Space API Remoting for Secure Containers in Public Clouds
paper.abstract: In public cloud environments, secure containers face challenges in device virtualization due to their micro virtual machine architecture. We introduce Mercury, a user-space API remoting framework co-designed with our secure container RunD. Mercury leverages a dynamic shared memory interface between guest and host, along with KVM hypercalls for efficient notifications. When applied to CUDA, Mercury preserves API semantics across virtualization boundaries, enabling GPU virtualization with under 4% overhead during large language model inference. Mercury also achieves a 20% speedup compared to existing API remoting solutions. Building on Mercury, we deploy GPU sharing and checkpoint/restore in Alibaba Cloud, effectively doubling GPU deployment density and reducing cold start latency by over 95% in practice.

paper.title: DySpin: A Plug-and-Play Library Advancing Dynamic Sparse Long-Context Inference
paper.abstract: Long-context LLM inference is constrained by the memory-bandwidth and capacity demands of the key-value (KV) cache. Existing sparse methods typically use fixed per-head token budgets, overlooking variations in runtime demand. Moreover, since they retain all tokens in memory, these methods do not alleviate GPU memory capacity constraints. To overcome these limitations, we present DySpin, a plug-and-play library for dynamic sparse long-context inference. Its training-free runtime allocator dynamically adjusts token budgets to preserve important tokens and improve accuracy. To address the resulting workload imbalance, FastEstimate fuses token-importance evaluation and selection to generate scheduling indices that guide a specialized decoding attention kernel for fine-grained load balancing. DySpin further employs six-bit KV cache quantization and a novel packing format that enables register-level parallel unpacking and dequantization, reducing both dequantization overhead and memory footprint. DySpin integrates with existing sparse frameworks, improving accuracy while reducing long-context inference latency and KV cache memory usage.

paper.title: SwarmLoRA: Serverless Shared-Computation Disaggregation for Isolated, High-Throughput Multi-LoRA Serving
paper.abstract: Over 100,000 public LoRA adapters now share a small number of base LLMs, and cloud providers increasingly serve them for independent tenants whose private data must stay isolated. Serverful systems co-locate all adapters in one process for efficient batching but sacrifice isolation; serverless systems run each adapter in an isolated function but redundantly recompute the shared base-model projection in every one, wasting GPU memory bandwidth. We present SwarmLoRA, a disaggregated serverless architecture that separates shared computation from per-adapter state. A persistent aggregator batches the base-model projection once across all active functions; isolated worker functions each hold one adapter’s weights and KV cache and scale independently. This design achieves cross-adapter batching without breaking per-adapter isolation. SwarmLoRA achieves 4.1×-4.9× higher throughput on four L40S GPUs than state-of-the-art ServerlessLLM and ServerlessLoRA, while preventing cross-tenant data leakage through malicious adapters. SwarmLoRA shows that multi-tenant LoRA serving need not trade tenant isolation for batching efficiency.

paper.title: CoCoDiff: Optimizing Collective Communications for Distributed Diffusion Transformer Inference Under Ulysses Sequence Parallelism
paper.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) are increasingly adopted in scientific computing, yet growing model sizes and resolutions make distributed multi-GPU inference essential. Ulysses sequence parallelism scales DiT inference but introduces frequent all-to-all collectives that dominate latency. Overlapping these with computation is difficult due to tight data dependencies, large messages, and asymmetric interconnect bandwidths. We introduce CoCoDiff, a distributed DiT inference engine exploiting two observations: (1) V requires only linear projection while Q/K need additional normalization and RoPE, enabling overlap of V's communication with Q/K computation; (2) adjacent denoising steps produce similar tensors, yielding temporal redundancy. CoCoDiff introduces three mechanisms: Tile-Aware Parallel All-to-all (TAPA) decomposes collectives into topology-aligned phases; V-First scheduling hides V's communication behind Q/K computation; and V-Major selective communication transmits only active projections on slow interconnects. On Aurora with four DiT models across 1–8 nodes (up to 96 Intel GPU tiles), CoCoDiff achieves an average speedup of 3.6×, peaking at 8.4×.

paper.title: Maze: A Distributed Framework for Large Language Model Agents
paper.abstract: LLM agents are transitioning from single-node to large-scale, multi-tenant services. A user request no longer corresponds to a single inference call, but to a long-running workflow interleaving heterogeneous tasks. Existing agent systems struggle with these workloads due to resource-blind, coarse-grained placement or ignore agentic workload awareness. We present Maze, a distributed agent framework bridging the abstraction gap from agentic logic to fine-grained task-level deployment. At its core, Maze anchors task resource semantics and introduces Heterogeneity-Aware Criticality Scheduler, a scheduler leveraging agentic workload features and value-density scoring to prioritize valuable agentic workflows and critical tasks while eliminating cross-resource head-of-line blocking. Coupled with elastic inference engine scaling, zero-VRAM optimizations, and closed-loop fault tolerance, Maze ensures a robust, performant runtime. Evaluation on diverse workloads demonstrates that Maze achieves up to 2.9x higher throughput, reduces P95 latency by 54.2%, and increases GPU utilization by 50% compared to state-of-the-art frameworks.

paper.title: ZOCheck: CPU-Shadow Checkpointing for Zeroth-Order LLM Fine-Tuning
paper.abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization is an attractive option for memory-efficient LLM fine-tuning, but its fault tolerance remains underexplored. Unlike first-order training, ZO progress can be represented by lightweight seed-and-scalar step logs, yet naive log-only recovery still incurs replay cost that grows with training progress, and shortcut replay does not preserve the executed floating-point trajectory. We present ZOCheck, a fault-tolerant ZO training system that exploits this replayable structure through a CPU shadow process that continuously replays logged updates, materializes consistent recovery images off the GPU critical path, and persists them asynchronously. ZOCheck combines non-blocking checkpointing with fast recovery from a near-current state. We also develop a cost model for choosing the snapshot policy under realistic failure rates. Experiments show that ZOCheck reduces checkpoint overhead by up to 219.7× and recovery latency by 1.55× on average over asynchronous full-state checkpointing, yielding up to 21.3× lower end-to-end wasted time while preserving exact recovery behavior.

paper.title: Evaluation and Optimization of Communication Compression for 10K-GPU LLM Training
paper.abstract: Collective communication is critical for scaling large language model (LLM) training to megascale GPU clusters. However, communication becomes a major bottleneck limiting scalability. Existing approaches improve bandwidth utilization but are constrained by the physical network in large-scale clusters. Communication compression reduces data volume and offers a way to break the communication wall, yet its performance and accuracy at extreme scale remain unclear. To bridge this gap, we present the first systematic study of communication compression across scales up to 10K GPUs, showing that it maintains accuracy but suffers from limited performance gains due to bandwidth hierarchy limitations, weak communication scaling, and limited resource awareness. We enhance the co-design of communication and compression with a hierarchical method that restructures communication compression, adapts communication algorithms to each scale, and tunes network resource allocation. Our approach achieves up to 5.87x communication improvement and 1.73x end-to-end training speedup on Llama3 models at 10,240 GPUs.

paper.title: Pushing the Limits of Structured Sparse GEMM on Hopper GPUs via Analytical Modeling
paper.abstract: Structured sparsity improves performance in LLM inference and scientific computing, yet Hopper 2:4 sparse GEMM remains poorly understood. Published kernel-level optimizations target older architectures, while no prior work investigates how Hopper's Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA), warpgroup execution, expanded shared memory, and asynchronous pipelines reshape the design space. We present an analytical model that captures roofline bounds, L2 reuse, pipeline overlap, and wave quantization for Hopper sparse GEMM. It serves as a guardrail for configuration search. Guided by the model, we develop an auto-tuned kernel combining warp-specialized TMA pipelining, metadata prepacking, barrier-decomposed overlap, and per-operand swizzles. On an H800 PCIe GPU, it outperforms cuSPARSELt on 80 of 95 shapes (84%) under identical problem configurations, with mean speedup of +16.7% and up to 1.4x. The model identifies memory bottlenecks and narrows the configuration space before compilation, reducing tuning cost while retaining high-performance configurations. This paper bridges both gaps.

paper.title: BatchFlow: Benefit-Aware Data Pipeline Allocation and Batch Reuse for Multi-Job Training
paper.abstract: Deep learning training is often limited by data pipeline throughput, reducing accelerator utilization and increasing training time and cost. This is particularly challenging in multi-tenant environments, where jobs compete for storage and CPU resources. We present BatchFlow, a data pipeline service that improves aggregate training throughput by dynamically allocating data pipeline workers across jobs. BatchFlow uses online profiling to estimate how quickly each job consumes mini-batches and how quickly workers can prepare them, then allocates workers to jobs where data supply is most likely to fall behind training demand. BatchFlow also caches prepared mini-batches for reuse across jobs, reducing repeated reads from slow storage and redundant CPU preprocessing. When cache capacity is limited, a benefit-aware policy determines which mini-batches to prefetch and retain. Across multi-job workloads, BatchFlow increases aggregate training throughput by up to 3.8× and cost efficiency by up to 2.1× relative to prior systems.

paper.title: DiffSpec: Accelerating Long Sequence Generation with Differential Speculative Decoding
paper.abstract: Long sequence generation is a critical workload for large language model (LLM) inference, but its high computational cost limits scalable deployment. Existing speculative decoding methods accelerate inference by verifying multiple draft tokens per step, yet uniform speculation concentrates failures in late decoding stages, where marginal payoff is highest, reducing overall speedup. We propose DiffSpec, a differential speculative decoding framework that adapts speculation to position-specific utility. At the algorithmic level, DiffSpec employs utility-guided draft construction with relevance-aware key-value (KV) selection and adaptive draft tree construction, improving candidate quality in high-impact regions. At the system level, a differential speculative execution engine supports utility-adaptive speculation via reuse-aware KV residency and topology-aware fused verification, handling irregular KV cache accesses and heterogeneous workloads. Experiments on four NVIDIA H100 GPUs with sequences up to 128K tokens show end-to-end speedups of 7.72×, 3.45×, and 2.36× over EAGLE-3, TriForce, and MagicDec, respectively.

paper.title: Spec-K: Adaptive Resource Allocation via Speculative Preview for Efficient MoE Inference
paper.abstract: Inference serving for large language models (LLMs) often relies on static resource allocation—such as fixed Top-k routing in mixture-of-experts (MoE) models—despite substantial token-level heterogeneity. This mismatch causes systematic over-provisioning, magnified in long reasoning and batched speculative decoding. We introduce Resource Allocation via Speculative Preview (RASP), a framework that leverages predictive signals from a draft model to guide token-level allocation before target-model verification, enabling fine-grained adjustment of compute budgets to match instantaneous demand. As an instantiation, Spec-K applies RASP to MoE routing: it uses speculative preview to estimate token uncertainty and reallocates the Top-k budget dynamically via a minimalist policy, reducing expert computation, communication traffic, and activated expert count in batched verification—thereby improving throughput and even speculative acceptance. Experiments on distributed MoE inference show that Spec-K achieves up to 1.72× end-to-end throughput improvement over a strong baseline, with negligible accuracy loss on complex reasoning and instruction-following tasks.

paper.title: TIDE: Temporal Incremental Draft Engine for Self-Improving LLM Inference
paper.abstract: Speculative decoding can substantially accelerate LLM inference, but realizing its benefits in practice is challenging due to evolving workloads. We present TIDE (Temporal Incremental Draft Engine), a serving-engine-native framework that integrates online draft adaptation directly into high-performance LLM inference systems. TIDE reuses target model's intermediate hidden states generated during inference as training signals for draft adaptation, thereby avoiding additional target model computation and serving-time overhead. It employs adaptive runtime control to activate speculation and draft model training only when beneficial. TIDE exploits heterogeneous clusters by mapping inference and training to appropriate GPU classes. Across diverse real-world workloads, TIDE achieves up to 1.66× throughput over no-speculation baselines while recovering performance on misaligned workloads where static draft models degrade throughput. TIDE also reduces training time by up to 3.02× and storage requirements by 24× compared to existing draft training approaches, and improves system throughput by up to 1.22× on heterogeneous GPU clusters.

paper.title: LLMProf: Identifying Performance Bottlenecks in LLM Serving Systems with Top-Down Profiling
paper.abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving systems have become critical cloud workloads, yet their performance diagnosis remains challenging due to rapid software-hardware evolution, dynamic request patterns, and the limitations of existing profiling tools. These gaps force developers to rely on manual heuristics for performance optimization, leading to slow progress and error-prone code. We present LLMProf, a low-overhead profiling framework tailored for various LLM serving systems. LLMProf employs a top-down, multi-level analysis approach that captures only the most relevant metrics at each profiling level to balance detail with minimal performance impact while remaining agnostic to frameworks and hardware. We present case studies that leverage LLMProf to optimize real-world LLM serving workloads, from which we derive a performance diagnosis taxonomy that provides actionable guidance and enables automated postmortem analysis. Our case studies demonstrate that by applying simple optimizations uncovered by LLMProf, we can achieve up to 2.09× throughput improvement.
